{{Short description|Scottish mathematician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2017}}
{{Use British English|date=February 2017}}
[[File:William Galbraith's grave, Grange Cemetery.JPG|thumb|William Galbraith's grave, Grange Cemetery]]

Rev '''William Galbraith''' (1786 – 27 October 1850) was a Scottish mathematician. He taught mathematics and nautical astronomy in Edinburgh, and took an interest in surveying work, becoming an advocate of the extension of the work of [[Principal Triangulation of Great Britain|triangulating Great Britain]].<ref name=NMS>{{Cite web|url=http://nms.scran.ac.uk/database/record.php?usi=000-190-002-067-C|title=National Museums of Scotland - Rule (Detail)}}</ref>

==Early life==
He was born at [[Greenlaw]], [[Berwickshire]].<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1851MNRAS..11...86.|bibcode = 1851MNRAS..11...86.|title = Biographical notices of Mr. William Galbraith|journal = Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|year = 1851|volume = 11|issue=4|page = 86|doi = 10.1093/mnras/11.4.67a <!-- full article, not just page 86 -->|doi-access = free}}</ref> Initially he was a schoolmaster. His pupil
[[William Rutherford (mathematician)|William Rutherford]] walked long distances to attend his school at [[Eccles, Berwickshire|Eccles]]. Subsequently, he moved to Edinburgh, and graduated A.M. at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1821.<ref name="Society1851">{{cite book|author=Royal Astronomical Society|title=Memoirs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gC80AQAAIAAJ&pg=PA194|access-date=6 November 2012|year=1851|publisher=Society|pages=194–}}</ref>

==Surveyor==
During the 1830s Galbraith became interested in the surveying problems of Scotland. In 1831 he pointed out that [[Arthur's Seat]] had a strongly magnetic peak.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www20.us.archive.org/stream/topographicalsta01edinuoft#page/n145/mode/2up|title = The topographical, statistical, and historical gazetteer of Scotland|year = 1848}}</ref> In 1837 he pointed out the impact of anomalies in measurement, work that received recognition;<ref>{{Cite book|last=Kaiserl. Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien|url=http://archive.org/details/almanachderkais03wiengoog|title=Almanach der Kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften für das Jahr ..|date=1851|publisher=Wien : K.K. Hof- und Staatsdruckerei|others=Harvard University}}</ref> it was topical because of the 1836 geological map of Scotland by [[John MacCulloch]], with which critics had found fault on topographical as well as geological grounds.<ref>{{ODNBweb|id=17412|title=MacCulloch, John|first=David A.|last=Cumming}}</ref> A paper on the locations of places on the [[River Clyde]] was recognised in 1837 by a gold medal, from the Society for the Encouragement of the Useful Arts for Scotland.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Edinburgh Philosophical Journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U3JQAAAAcAAJ&pg=RA1-PA219|access-date=6 November 2012|year=1837|publisher=Constable|pages=1–}}</ref>

Galbraith followed with detailed ''Remarks on the Geographical Position of some Points on the West Coast of Scotland'' (1838).<ref>{{cite book|title=The Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B1sEAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA300|access-date=4 May 2012|year=1838|publisher=A. and C. Black|pages=300–}}</ref> Having made some accurate surveys of his own, he lobbied for further attention from the national survey.<ref name=NMS/>
[[File:Pocket box circle Galbraith.png|thumb|Galbraith's pocket-box circle, an invention for portable surveying.]]

==Later life==
About 1832 Galbraith was licensed a minister by the presbytery of [[Dunse]]. He married Eleanor Gale in 1833.<ref name="Society1851"/>

Galbraith was buried with his wife in the north-east section of the [[Grange, Edinburgh|Grange Cemetery]] in [[Edinburgh]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/monumentsmonumen01rogeiala#page/152/mode/2up|title = Monuments and monumental inscriptions in Scotland}}</ref>

==Works==
Galbraith's major works combined textbook material with mathematical tables:

*''Mathematical and Astronomical Tables'' (1827):<ref name="Galbraith1827">{{cite book|author=William Galbraith|title=Mathematical and Astronomical Tables|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z-MzmqlIfUsC|access-date=4 May 2012|year=1827}}</ref> review.<ref name="JamesonJardine1827">{{cite book|author1=Robert Jameson|author2=Sir William Jardine|author3=Henry Darwin Rogers|title=The Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal: exhibiting a view of the progressive discoveries and improvements in the sciences and the arts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0AwXAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA404|access-date=4 May 2012|year=1827|publisher=A. and C. Black|pages=404–}}</ref>
*''Trigonometrical Surveying, Levelling, and Railway Engineering'' (1842)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/trigonometrical00galbgoog#page/n6/mode/2up|title=Trigonometrical surveying, levelling, and railway engineering|year=1842}}</ref>

He edited [[John Ainslie]]'s 1812 treatise on land surveying (1849),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/atreatiseonland00ainsgoog|title = A treatise on land surveying &#91;ed.&#93; by W. Galbraith|year = 1849}}</ref> and with William Rutherford revised [[John Bonnycastle]]'s ''Algebra''.<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Rutherford, William}}</ref>
